title: Investigating Why Petri Elicits More Deception from Some Models Than Others
original_idea: Use Petri's open-source code on open-weight models. Correlate deception rates with training data composition, RLHF method, model size, and architecture.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Good theory: identifying training practices that predict deception rates directly informs safer training pipelines and deployment risk assessment.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Petri is open-source, which lowers the barrier. However, running it on multiple models and doing correlation analysis with training practices requires both compute and knowledge of model training details that beginners may lack.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Very broad: running Petri on a range of models, collecting training metadata, and doing multivariate correlation analysis. The correlation with training data composition is particularly hard since training details for many models are undisclosed.

novelty.reasoning: Petri is an open-source tool by Anthropic that has already been applied to 14 frontier models with 111 seed instructions, and Petri 2.0 expanded this further. Anthropic has published model comparisons showing variation in deception rates across models and domains. However, the specific proposal to correlate deception rates with training data composition, RLHF method, model size, and architecture has not been systematically published. The main challenge is that training details for most models are undisclosed, limiting feasibility. DeceptionBench (arxiv 2510.15501) provides domain-level analysis of deception variation.
